messages.subject: Two questions about nimble
parts:
Hi,

I have two questions.

First, how to convert following jags code into nimble:
The precision matrix is just inverse of correlation matrix with correlations all equal.

model{
for(i in 1:len){
  p[i]<-phi(vi[s[i],t[i]])
  r[i]~dbin(p[i],totaln[i])
}
for(j in 1:nstudy){
  vi[j,1:ntrt]~dmnorm(mu,T[1:ntrt,1:ntrt])
}
for(j in 1:ntrt){
  AR[j]<-phi(mu[j]/sqrt(1+pow(sigma,2)))
  mu[j]~dnorm(0,0.001)
}
sigma~dunif(0.0001,c)
for(j in 1:ntrt){
  for(k in 1:ntrt){
   T[j,k]<-1/sigma^2*ifelse(j==k,diag,offdiag)
  }
}

diag<-(1+(ntrt-2)*rho)/(1+(ntrt-2)*rho-(ntrt-1)*rho^2)
offdiag<-(-rho/(1+(ntrt-2)*rho-(ntrt-1)*rho^2))
rho~dunif(-1/(ntrt-1),0.9999)
}

Second,
The nimble has too many different mcmc,model, build functions. They made me confused.
Are there any function in nimble similar as following two functions in stan?

compiled_model <- stan_model(model_code)
fit <- sampling(compiled_model,pars=monitor.var,data=data.stan,init=init.stan,
                  chains=4,iter=3000,warmup=1000,verbose=TRUE,seed=(666+job),thin=1)


Thanks
Simon

messages.subject: Re: Two questions about nimble
parts:
As far as setting up your model in NIMBLE, we don't provide ifelse() for use in model code. Instead, the best thing to do is write a 
user-defined function that would fill in the values of T. This would have the great benefit of avoiding creating nodes in the model
graph for each element of T. Instead the function would fill in T and the entire T matrix would be treated as one node, which would
speed up various aspects of the computation. At the bottom of this email, I show an example of a user defined function for specifying
a covariance matrix in a Gaussian process setting. Hopefully it will be straightforward for you to modify that code for your case. 

As far as a single function to run an MCMC, please see information on the nimbleMCMC function in our user manual or help(nimbleMCMC).
This allows you to take code for a model (or an existing model) and just run an MCMC without the intermediate steps, if you don't have
any interest in making modifications to the MCMC as is possible in the intermediate steps.

-chris


expcov <- nimbleFunction(    
   run = function(dists = double(2), rho = double(0), sigma = double(0)) {
      returnType(double(2))
      n <- dim(dists)[1]
      result <- matrix(nrow = n, ncol = n, init = FALSE)
      sigma2 <- sigma*sigma
      for(i in 1:n)
            for(j in 1:n)
                  result[i, j] <- sigma2*exp(-dists[i,j]/rho)
      return(result)
})

code <- nimbleCode({
     mu0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
     sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)  
     rho ~ dunif(0, 5)
     beta ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
 
     mu[1:N] <- mu0*ones[1:N]
     cov[1:N, 1:N] <- expcov(dists[1:N, 1:N], rho, sigma)  
     # dists is a (constant) matrix of pairwise distances between spatial locations
     s[1:N] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:N], cov = cov[1:N, 1:N])
     # likelihood
     for(i in 1:N) {
        lambda[i] <- exp(log(expected[i]) + beta*x[i] + s[i])
        y[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    }
})
```

parts:
Hi Simon,

In your nimble code you define the covariance using the nimbleFunction. In your jags code you define the precision (T).
It's not clear to me that those two definitions specify the same model (i.e., is the covariance you construct equal
to the inverse of T? 

I would think the easiest thing to do is set up the nimbleFunction so that it constructs the T matrix equivalently
to what you have in your model code for the jags implementation.

As far as not recompiling, you can always access and modify model variables in the compiled model like a typical R object.  
If cModel is a compiled model, you can say

cModel$my_data <- some_new_values
cModel$my_covariate <- some_other_new_values

etc.  Then you can run whatever algorithm you want on the model with the revised values. 

-chris

As far as setting up your model in NIMBLE, we don't provide ifelse() for use in model code. Instead, the best thing to do is write a 
user-defined function that would fill in the values of T. This would have the great benefit of avoiding creating nodes in the model
graph for each element of T. Instead the function would fill in T and the entire T matrix would be treated as one node, which would
speed up various aspects of the computation. At the bottom of this email, I show an example of a user defined function for specifying
a covariance matrix in a Gaussian process setting. Hopefully it will be straightforward for you to modify that code for your case. 

As far as a single function to run an MCMC, please see information on the nimbleMCMC function in our user manual or help(nimbleMCMC).
This allows you to take code for a model (or an existing model) and just run an MCMC without the intermediate steps, if you don't have
any interest in making modifications to the MCMC as is possible in the intermediate steps.

-chris


expcov <- nimbleFunction(    
   run = function(dists = double(2), rho = double(0), sigma = double(0)) {
      returnType(double(2))
      n <- dim(dists)[1]
      result <- matrix(nrow = n, ncol = n, init = FALSE)
      sigma2 <- sigma*sigma
      for(i in 1:n)
            for(j in 1:n)
                  result[i, j] <- sigma2*exp(-dists[i,j]/rho)
      return(result)
})

code <- nimbleCode({
     mu0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
     sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)  
     rho ~ dunif(0, 5)
     beta ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
 
     mu[1:N] <- mu0*ones[1:N]
     cov[1:N, 1:N] <- expcov(dists[1:N, 1:N], rho, sigma)  
     # dists is a (constant) matrix of pairwise distances between spatial locations
     s[1:N] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:N], cov = cov[1:N, 1:N])
     # likelihood
     for(i in 1:N) {
        lambda[i] <- exp(log(expected[i]) + beta*x[i] + s[i])
        y[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    }
})
```

hi Simon,

I looked at some output from jags and nimble when using
`non_missing_pattern <- missing_pattern_determine(event)`, and the
MCMC
output looks similar to me between jags and nimble. So I'm not sure
what you're seeing when you say they give different results.

Side note (but potentially helpful for improving computational
efficiency): it is best to set 's' and 't' in 'constants' rather than
in 'data'.
Otherwise nimble thinks that the dependency structure can change
because 's' and 't' could change, which can result in additional
unneeded calculations. You can also set 'totaln' in constants.

As far as the second question, if you are changing constants (in
particular the number of items in a for loop or the size of any
variables)
then you would need to recreate the model and recompile. If you are
only changing values of data or covariates (specified via 'inits' or
'data', not 'constants')
then you could do as I suggested. You might be able to arrange things
so that you group simulations that have the same sizes and only
recompile when you need to change sizes.

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

Cmodel$varName <- some_value
Cmcmc$run(1000)

Cmodel$varName <- some_other_value
## you may want to think at this point about what initial values you
want for the MCMC and possibly reset the relevant parameter values
Cmcmc$run(1000)

-chris

>>>> As far as setting up your model in NIMBLE, we don't provide ifelse() for use in model code. Instead, the best thing to do is write a
>>>> user-defined function that would fill in the values of T. This would have the great benefit of avoiding creating nodes in the model
>>>> graph for each element of T. Instead the function would fill in T and the entire T matrix would be treated as one node, which would
>>>> speed up various aspects of the computation. At the bottom of this email, I show an example of a user defined function for specifying
>>>> a covariance matrix in a Gaussian process setting. Hopefully it will be straightforward for you to modify that code for your case.
>>>>
>>>> As far as a single function to run an MCMC, please see information on the nimbleMCMC function in our user manual or help(nimbleMCMC).
>>>> This allows you to take code for a model (or an existing model) and just run an MCMC without the intermediate steps, if you don't have
>>>> any interest in making modifications to the MCMC as is possible in the intermediate steps.
>>>>
>>>> -chris
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> expcov <- nimbleFunction(
>>>> run = function(dists = double(2), rho = double(0), sigma = double(0)) {
>>>> returnType(double(2))
>>>> n <- dim(dists)[1]
>>>> result <- matrix(nrow = n, ncol = n, init = FALSE)
>>>> sigma2 <- sigma*sigma
>>>> for(i in 1:n)
>>>> for(j in 1:n)
>>>> result[i, j] <- sigma2*exp(-dists[i,j]/rho)
>>>> return(result)
>>>> })
>>>>
>>>> code <- nimbleCode({
>>>> mu0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
>>>> sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)
>>>> rho ~ dunif(0, 5)
>>>> beta ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
>>>>
>>>> mu[1:N] <- mu0*ones[1:N]
>>>> cov[1:N, 1:N] <- expcov(dists[1:N, 1:N], rho, sigma)
>>>> # dists is a (constant) matrix of pairwise distances between spatial locations
>>>> s[1:N] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:N], cov = cov[1:N, 1:N])
>>>> # likelihood
>>>> for(i in 1:N) {
>>>> lambda[i] <- exp(log(expected[i]) + beta*x[i] + s[i])
>>>> y[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
>>>> }
>>>> })
>>>> ```
